guard: a session's durable event state is released on a lifetime the connector states: the principal lock at the final teardown, a thread's write-ahead log only once it can no longer answer a recovery
why: #599 is two halves and only one of them is visible on the wire. The swap that this PR serialized
closes the predecessor's run and binds the replacement holder, which is a complete account of
what an OBSERVER sees. It says nothing about the lock and the log the session created on disk,
and those were both left behind: the connector destructured the location `ensureEventWalDir`
returns and dropped the held lock, so no `release()` was called anywhere in shipped source, and
no path removed a retired thread's directory. The suite this table grades is the one that watches
the disk rather than the subject.
W1 IS THE LOCK, AND ITS REACHABLE OUTCOME IS A REFUSED REPLACEMENT. `dispose` is the editor
unloading the plugin, not the host exiting, so the pid the lock recorded is still alive when the
next process starts. `acquirePrincipalLock` refuses a live owner on this host by design, which is
the right answer to the question it was asked and the wrong outcome here, because the owner it
names stopped publishing at dispose. Reproduced across two processes before the cells existed.
THE PROCESS ARM CANNOT BE FOLDED INTO THE IN-PROCESS ONE. `acquirePrincipalLock` deliberately
returns the SAME lock object to a second caller inside one process, because a `/new` under one
principal must not be refused. A same-process replacement is therefore answered by that cache and
would grade nothing at all, which is why W1 is aimed at the in-process teardown cell it reddens
FIRST and the process cells stand behind it as the reachable consequence.
W2 AND W3 ARE THE SAME LIFETIME FROM ITS TWO SIDES, and one without the other proves the wrong
thing. A log exists so a later start can recover what its thread had not yet published, so
'removed' is not the property, WHEN is. W2 stops reaping at all and the accumulation #599 names
comes straight back: one directory per `/new`, forever. W3 reaps unconditionally, which passes any
cell that only watches for the directory to disappear while destroying the log of a drain that
spent its bound and is, by this connector's own design, still uncancelled and possibly writing.
A suite with only W2's cell would call W3's connector correct.
THE ABANDONED ARM COSTS TWELVE SECONDS AND THAT IS NOT PADDING. The hold has to exceed
`SWAP_SETTLE_MS`, or the drain settles, the reap arm runs twice, and the keep cell grades nothing.
SPECIFIER BOUNDARY: the suite imports `../src/plugin.js` under tsx and the probe boots the same
source, so the bytes mutated are the bytes executed. `@cotal-ai/connector-core` resolves to its
source through the workspace link rather than to a dist, so no build is prepended and no
`afterRestore` rebuild is needed.
W4 IS THE OTHER HALF OF THE LIFETIME, and it exists because a first draft of this table said the
arm was unreachable. It is not. A frame reaches the log only through `beginSend`, and everything
ahead of that has to succeed: `splitFrames` asks the endpoint for `maxPayload`, which is read off
the client's cached server INFO and throws once the client has processed the close, because nats.js
nulls `protocol.info` on its first reconnect dial.
SO KILLING THE BROKER IS A RACE, AND BOTH SIDES OF IT ARE REAL. Reach `beginSend` before the client
processes the close and the frame IS frozen, the publish then failing on its ack timeout, which is
the state this arm wants. Lose that race and the pump dies on the payload read with nothing ever
pending. Both have been observed against the real plugin on this same scenario, differing only in
timing. An earlier version of this note reported only the second and called it what a SIGKILL does,
which stated one side of a race as a certainty: worse than a gap, because the next reader builds on
it. Recorded here because the correction came from a reviewer's live probe rather than from re-reading.
WHAT REMOVES THE RACE is a link that stops delivering without closing. The client is never told, so
`maxPayload` keeps answering from cache, the pump always reaches `beginSend`, and only the ack fails
to come back. The suite puts a relay in front of its own broker and cuts it for exactly that reason:
a cell that grades whichever side of a race it landed on is not a cell.
THE KEEP DIRECTION IS THE SAFE ONE, so this was a coverage gap on a reachable arm rather than a
product defect: the connector already did the right thing and nothing graded that it did. W4 makes
the reap ignore the pending frame, which deletes the only copy of a frame whose fate nobody knows.

mutations.cell: teardown gives the principal's lock back
mutations.note: The defect exactly as it shipped: the lock was taken, used correctly, and never handed back. Nothing else changes: the seat still runs, still publishes, still tears down cleanly, and the only trace is a file whose record names a live pid.

mutations.note: The plausible over-repair, and the reason the lifetime is graded rather than the deletion. It passes W2's cell and every directory-count reading of 'the predecessor was cleaned up'.
